articles.title: Delta to prosecute businesses without CCTV cameras The Delta State Government has warned business owners and public institutions that failure to install closed-circuit television cameras on their premises could attract prosecution under the state’s law. The Permanent Secretary and Solicitor-General of the Ministry of Justice, Omamuzo Erebe, said the government would soon move from public sensitisation to enforcing the relevant provisions. Erebe gave the warning on Thursday during the 2027 budget bilateral discussions involving ministries, departments and agencies, organised by the Ministry of Economic Planning in Asaba. He urged business operators and heads of public institutions to install CCTV cameras, saying the equipment would improve security and help protect lives and property. “I want to use this opportunity to advise business owners and public institutions to ensure that they install CCTV cameras on their premises. “It does not cost as much as people think, and it helps protect society. The law was not enacted just for the sake of having legislation; it is meant to be obeyed. “Very soon, some people may face prosecution for failing to comply with the relevant provisions,” he said. Erebe maintained that ignorance of the law would not exempt anyone from compliance, adding that the government was prepared to take action against defaulters. Reviewing the ministry’s performance in 2026, he said it had recorded progress in defending cases involving the state and reducing unnecessary litigation. He attributed the improvement to better legal advice to ministries, departments and agencies, as well as regular training and motivation for government lawyers. The Solicitor-General disclosed that the ministry had introduced a reward system for lawyers who successfully handled cases, saying the initiative had encouraged improved performance. He added that the ministry had trained officials of government agencies, including the Ministries of Lands and Surveys and Commerce, to ensure that their activities complied with legal requirements. Erebe identified land acquisition as an area where government agencies needed to observe due process, noting that newspaper publications alone might not satisfy the legal requirements. He said the relevant parties must also be properly served to prevent disputes arising from land acquisition. On the ministry’s request for additional lawyers in the 2027 budget, Erebe said the shortage of legal professionals had made fresh recruitment necessary to strengthen its capacity. “The shortage of legal professionals is not limited to the medical sector. It is also happening in the legal profession. That is why we made a case for additional recruitment of lawyers into the ministry,” he said. He described Delta State’s Administration of Criminal Justice Law as one of the most modern legal frameworks, adding that the ministry was reviewing existing laws to address gaps and ensure they reflected current realities. The latest warning followed an earlier directive by the state government in September 2024 reminding owners of commercial premises and public places to comply with the CCTV installation requirement. The government said the law had been in operation since July 28, 2020 and covered facilities including shopping malls, eateries, cinemas, supermarkets, petrol stations, hotels, offices, worship centres and schools. At the time, the government said non-compliance could attract a two-year prison term, a fine of ₦500,000 and the sealing of affected premises until the required cameras were installed.

articles.title: Washington Commanders Face New York Giants in Rematch
articles.summary: The Washington Commanders will look to bounce back from their previous loss against the New York Giants.
articles.content: The Washington Commanders will be looking to bounce back from a disappointing loss when they face off against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on Thursday night. The game marks a rematch of their Week 5 encounter, which was a frustrating experience for many Commanders fans. In that game, the Commanders held a seemingly insurmountable 14-point lead in the fourth quarter, only to see it slip away due to a series of unfortunate events. Cornerback Amik Robertson's interception of Jameis Winston was initially thought to have sealed the win for Washington, but a penalty call negated the play and gave the Giants another chance. The Giants took full advantage of the second opportunity, scoring on the very next play. They continued to pile on points, forcing the game into overtime. Just as it seemed that New York was about to emerge victorious with a game-winning field goal attempt, running back Cam Skattebo fumbled the ball, handing the Commanders a lifeline. The remainder of the game saw Jayden Daniels lead his team down the field in pursuit of a potential game-winning score, only to see time run out as he was tackled. The loss left many wondering what could have been for the Commanders, who had previously beaten only one opponent this season - the Eagles. The Commanders are set to face off against the New York Giants, who have undergone significant changes since their last meeting. One key difference is at quarterback, where JJ McCarthy will take the helm instead of Jameis Winston. McCarthy's presence under center allows the Giants to utilize a wider range of plays, including RPOs and designed quarterback runs that exploit his mobility. This dynamic also enables him to make quick decisions when necessary, whether it be escaping pressure or throwing downfield. As a result, McCarthy is more likely to throw into tight coverage than Winston was. The Giants' running game has been a mixed bag this season, with the team struggling to establish a consistent ground attack despite having aspirations of being a strong suit. While McCarthy's arrival may help in this regard, it's unlikely to single-handedly transform the unit, given the challenges posed by the interior offensive line and subpar run blocking grades. The Giants' running game has been hindered by issues with their interior O-line, which has struggled to open up holes for their backs. This weakness has seen them rank near the bottom of the league in terms of run-blocking efficiency. The New York Giants' offense has struggled to find consistency, partly due to issues with run-blocking efficiency, which has them ranked near the bottom of the league. Beyond Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely, there are other receivers to watch out for in the Giants' lineup. Rookie Malachi Fields has been a pleasant surprise, improving each week and providing an outlet when Nabers and Likely are covered. Fields is a unique athlete with skills that set him apart from others on the team. He excels in the red zone and endzone, and his height makes him a threat on 50-50 balls. Additionally, he's found a niche on third down, where he can be relied upon to make plays. The Giants' defense has shown improvement in recent weeks, but their run defense remains a concern. Despite the efforts of standout player Jalen Reader, Shelby Harris has been underwhelming and at times a liability. However, the team's biggest defensive strength lies in its coverage, with cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome playing at an elite level, particularly in man-to-man situations. The Washington Commanders' defense has found success in creating pressure on opposing quarterbacks through their blitz packages, even if they don't always record sacks. This approach disrupts the timing of the quarterback's play and forces them off their mark, leading to positive outcomes for the team. For Thursday's game against the New York Giants, it will be crucial for the Commanders' defense to execute this strategy effectively. articles.title: Conflict-Displaced Families Struggle to Feed Themselves in Kenya
articles.summary: Families fleeing violence in Ethiopia are finding safety in Kenya but struggling to feed their children due to ongoing fighting between Somali and Oromo communities.
articles.content: Mothers fleeing violence in Ethiopia are finding safety in Kenya but struggling to feed their children. The influx of refugees is due to ongoing fighting between Somali and Oromo communities in southern Ethiopia, which stems from a longstanding territorial dispute between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regional administrations. Families such as Shukria Dalacha's have been forced to leave everything behind, arriving in Kenya with little more than the clothes on their backs. We came here on foot late at night, running for our lives, she said. Dalacha, who gave birth to her daughter Sijra just before crossing into Kenya, is among those struggling to provide for her newborn's basic needs. The ongoing conflict in northern Tigray has left a trail of devastation in its wake, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation in Ethiopia. Researchers at Ghent University have estimated that approximately 500,000 civilians lost their lives between 2020 and 2022 due to violence, famine, and the collapse of essential health services. The instability is further compounded by the fact that communities are struggling to cope with drought, which has been exacerbated by conflict-related displacement. A recent assessment by regional and federal disaster authorities, as well as humanitarian partners, revealed that 3.9 million people in Tigray would require emergency food assistance through December. Displacement, restricted access to farmland, and disrupted livelihoods have all contributed to the severe impact of poor rains. Families continue to arrive at reception points in Kenya, where they are met with long lines and crowded registration areas. Hundreds of displaced individuals wait patiently for household rations and basic supplies, a testament to the overwhelming need for assistance. In one Kenyan host's home, 30 displaced people share a single room for sleeping, highlighting the severe shortage of accommodation. Kerko Mohammed, a 70-year-old woman, fled her home with her family after gunfire struck their walls during fighting between Somali and Oromo communities in Ethiopia. Her story is just one of many that illustrate the devastating effects of conflict on innocent civilians, who are forced to abandon their homes and livelihoods in search of safety. The influx of Ethiopian mothers seeking refuge in Kenya has brought about a new set of challenges, including finding enough food to feed their children. A Kenyan host had provided some relief by offering food and water, but the household's limited financial resources meant that the mothers were still struggling to make ends meet. In Marsabit County, local leaders had already been warning about the strain on resources due to impending food and water shortages, making it even more difficult for communities to accommodate the new arrivals. At the Al-Huda temporary camp, aid workers are doing their best to provide basic necessities, registering families and distributing supplies such as household rations and blankets. The number of Ethiopians seeking refuge in Kenya is staggering, with local authorities estimating that up to 50,000 people have crossed into the country since late October. Registration and verification efforts are ongoing, but aid agencies are struggling to keep pace with the influx of arrivals. The UNHCR has profiled around 14,000 individuals to establish their needs, but this is not a comprehensive count of those seeking assistance. The agency's limited financial resources mean that it cannot respond to the full extent of the crisis, with only $8.9 million requested in aid so far, although it remains unclear how much of this has been received. Her killing sparked a major scandal linked to former Prime Minister Najib Razak, who has repeatedly denied any involvement in the crime. Two members of an elite police unit, who were previously Najib's bodyguards, were convicted of Altantuya's murder. However, her lover Abdul Razak Baginda, a close aide to Najib, was acquitted of abetting the crime. Crucially, no one has ever been held accountable for ordering the killing. Mongolia's special envoy and member of a high-level government task force, Zandanshatar Gombojav, expressed regret over Malaysia's Court of Appeal decision in January. The court removed the Malaysian government's liability in a civil suit brought by Altantuya's family and reduced the damages awarded. The Mongolian government is seeking justice for Altantuya's family, who have been waiting for answers for 20 years. The diplomatic protest highlights the ongoing concerns about Malaysia's handling of this high-profile case, which has garnered international attention due to its connections to a former prime minister. A diplomatic protest note was sent by Mongolia to Malaysia on Tuesday, containing four key requests related to the 20-year-old murder case of Altantuya Shaariibuu. The note calls for a fair review of the court ruling in the case, as well as the return of one of the convicted officers who escaped to Australia so he can testify in the civil suit. Additionally, Mongolia has requested an examination of potentially new evidence that may be relevant to the case. An official written response from Malaysia is also being sought. The murder of Altantuya Shaariibuu, a translator for a former Malaysian defense minister, has been shrouded in controversy and speculation over the years. There have been claims that she was silenced to prevent her from exposing alleged corruption involving the purchase of submarines from France when Najib Razak was deputy premier and defense minister. The two policemen convicted of Altantuya's murder were sentenced to death, with one fleeing to Australia while appealing his conviction. The other had his sentence commuted to 40 years in prison in 2024 as part of a separate agreement. The family of Altantuya Shariibuu, a Mongolian national who was murdered in Malaysia 20 years ago, has continued to seek justice for her death despite numerous setbacks in the legal process. In an attempt to hold those responsible accountable, the family filed a civil suit against several defendants, including government officials and individuals involved in the case. A Malaysian high court initially ruled that these defendants were liable for damages and awarded the family 5 million ringgit ($1.2 million) in compensation in 2022. However, this decision was overturned by the Court of Appeal in January, which reduced the damages to 1.4 million ringgit ($343,000) and found that the conduct of the two policemen involved did not fall within their official duties. The family has since challenged this ruling, seeking a more favorable outcome. The case remains complicated due to allegations made by one of the accused police officers in Australia, who claimed that former Prime Minister Najib Razak ordered the killing. These claims have been denied by Najib, and it is unclear whether they will be established in court, but they continue to complicate efforts to bring those responsible for Altantuya's death to justice. articles.title: Israeli Airstrike on Hospital in Southern Gaza Kills At Least Six People
articles.summary: At least six people were killed when an Israeli airstrike targeted a hospital in southern Gaza, according to officials from the Palestinian enclave's health ministry.
articles.content: An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza has resulted in the deaths of at least six people, according to officials from the Palestinian enclave's health ministry. The strike targeted a surgery building at Nasser Hospital, where medical staff and patients were among those killed, the health ministry reported. The Israeli military claimed that its forces had been targeting a Hamas commander and other militants, but the hospital was a civilian facility with no apparent connection to the alleged targets. The impact of the strike has left destruction in its wake, including shattered ceilings and debris scattered throughout rooms at the hospital, which is one of the few remaining functioning medical facilities in Gaza after years of conflict. Among those killed was Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, a Palestinian surgeon who had been featured in the 2026 documentary "American Doctor" for his work providing medical care in Gaza. The Israeli military has accused Hamas of using Nasser Hospital in Gaza as a command center and storing weapons within its walls. According to the IDF, Hamas had established a presence inside the hospital complex and used it for interrogations and torture. Photos shared by the IDF appear to show weapons allegedly found within the medical facility. The claims are part of a long-standing dispute between Israel and Hamas over the use of hospitals in Gaza. The Israeli military has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating from within medical facilities, with both sides trading blame over the years. However, hospitals have protected status under international law, making them off-limits to attacks unless there is evidence that they are being used for military purposes. Despite this, several hospitals in Gaza have been targeted by Israeli forces during the ongoing conflict. Nasser Hospital itself has a history of being hit by Israeli strikes. In August 2025, it was hit by a double tap attack that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. The incident sparked widespread international condemnation and outrage over the targeting of civilians in medical facilities. The World Health Organization reports that Gaza's healthcare system has been severely damaged during Israel's yearslong offensive. Of the enclave's 37 hospitals, only two are considered fully functioning, while 18 are partially operational and 17 have ceased to function altogether. The data highlights the dire state of healthcare services in Gaza, where medical facilities are struggling to cope with the demands of a population under siege. The recent Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued unabated despite a ceasefire agreement reached last October, sparking renewed outrage among Palestinians. According to the Palestinian health ministry in the enclave, over 1,600 people have been killed since the truce came into effect, highlighting the dire consequences of ongoing violence. This figure is part of a larger toll that has seen more than 74,600 people lose their lives in Gaza since Israel's military operation began following Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023. The heavy rains and harsh winter conditions now gripping the enclave have only exacerbated the humanitarian crisis, prompting fresh calls for progress in peace negotiations between Israel and Hamas. articles.title: Apple's iPhone Launch Met with Skepticism in 2007
articles.summary: The highly anticipated Apple iPhone was met with skepticism when it first launched in 2007 due to its initial shortcomings.
articles.content: Apple's highly anticipated iPhone was met with skepticism when it first hit the market in 2007. Many experts doubted its chances of success, including Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer, who predicted that the iPhone would struggle to gain significant market share. The iPhone's initial shortcomings seemed insurmountable, from its touchscreen keyboard and limited app selection to its high price point and lack of essential features like corporate email support. PC Magazine columnist John C. Dvorak was particularly scathing in his criticism, suggesting that Apple should abandon the project altogether. Despite these warnings, Apple persevered and ultimately transformed the smartphone landscape. Today, the company is one of the world's leading tech giants, ranked fourth on the Fortune 500 list. The iPhone's success story serves as a reminder that initial doubts can often be misplaced. As we look to the future, similar skepticism surrounds the emergence of generative AI technology. Critics argue that it will struggle with technical flaws, high costs, and limited practical applications - all concerns that were raised against the iPhone when it first launched. In an interview on Fox News, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos expressed confidence in AI's potential to revolutionize productivity and change the way we work. He suggested that the technology could enable two-income households to live on a single paycheck or allow workers to support families with a three-day workweek. The notion that artificial intelligence will lead to widespread job losses is being challenged by tech mogul Jeff Bezos, who believes it could have a more profound impact on society. According to Bezos, AI will make it possible for families to live on one paycheck, rather than the current norm of two-income households. He predicts a labor shortage, where employers struggle to find workers due to their newfound flexibility and ability to work less. This shift in workforce dynamics is expected to be significant, with a substantial number of American couples having both parents working full-time in 2025. However, Bezos' vision suggests that this could change as AI takes over routine tasks, freeing up people to pursue more fulfilling careers or simply work fewer hours. Bezos has invested heavily in the development of AI through his startup Project Prometheus, which aims to make engineering and manufacturing processes easier and more accessible. He envisions a future where anyone can become an engineer with the aid of user-friendly tools and technology. Meanwhile, other experts are sounding alarm bells about the potential consequences of AI on employment rates. As the world grapples with the rapid advancements of artificial intelligence, two influential voices have emerged to challenge Jeff Bezos' optimistic forecast that AI could enable families to live on a single paycheck. Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has floated the idea of a four-day workweek, but in an essay he warned that the shift to AI will be one of the most turbulent times in human history and that world leaders are woefully unprepared for its risks. This stark warning highlights the complexity of the issue at hand, where technology is not only changing how tasks are performed but also who gets hired and which skills employers value. Critics point out a fundamental flaw in Bezos' prediction: productivity gains will only translate into shorter hours or a single-income lifestyle if savings from AI adoption reach employees. However, if companies choose to keep the benefits as profit or cut headcount, families may lose their second income without gaining any extra free time. This tension is evident within Amazon itself, where the company has axed around 30,000 corporate roles since late 2025 while planning to invest over $200 billion in capital spending this year. The debate surrounding AI's impact on employment and paychecks raises a crucial question: will the benefits of technological progress be shared among workers or siphoned off by corporations? As with the early iPhone critics who underestimated its potential, it remains unclear whether AI's gains will trickle down to employees' bank accounts or swell corporate coffers. articles.title: Supreme Court Ruling May Lead to Tariff Refunds for 330,000 Importers
articles.summary: A recent Supreme Court ruling against tariffs imposed under IEEPA has paved the way for importers to receive refunds, with over $115 billion already disbursed through Customs and Border Protection's CAPE system.
articles.content: U.S. importers may soon be eligible for a significant refund of tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), following a recent Supreme Court ruling against these levies. The Trump administration had sought to limit tariff refunds to only those importers who filed individual lawsuits against the government, but class counsel in a related case have now filed a motion with the U.S. Court of International Trade to enter a relief order that would automatically return money collected from tariffs to over 330,000 affected importers. This proposed order would grant the relevant agency the authority it claims is necessary to provide full refunds with interest to all class members, including small businesses that lack the resources to pursue their own cases. The ongoing struggle for American importers to receive tariff refunds has taken a significant step forward despite efforts by the Trump administration to limit these rebates. The affordability crisis that tariffs have exacerbated has had far-reaching consequences, including higher prices for consumers and financial strain on companies attempting to offset the costs of import taxes. The February Supreme Court ruling that tariffs imposed under IEEPA exceeded presidential powers paved the way for hundreds of billions of dollars in refunds to U.S. importers who bore the brunt of these levies. As of August, more than $115 billion has been disbursed back to American companies through Customs and Border Protection's CAPE system. However, many importers have yet to see their money returned due to various reasons. Some encountered technical errors in their CAPE submissions, while others lacked the necessary legal resources or failed to submit the required paperwork. Furthermore, small businesses and individuals who purchased tariffed items online often found themselves at a disadvantage compared to larger companies. This class action lawsuit, Freestyle World, Inc. v. United States, seeks to provide a pathway for these importers to receive their refunds without having to file individual lawsuits. The case is being heard in the U.S. Court of International Trade and was certified as a class action on October 8. The government's response to the initial complaint and motion for relief is now set to be filed by November 13. This timeline follows a recent development in the ongoing case involving universal tariff refunds. The Department of Justice will also need to respond to the motion for relief by December 9. Judge Richard Eaton, presiding over all tariff refund cases at the US Court of International Trade, has shown consistent support for universal rebates. His rulings have been instrumental in shaping the course of these proceedings. This is evident from his March decision granting refunds to importers who paid IEEPA tariffs. In a subsequent move, Judge Eaton issued a universal refund order, demonstrating his intention to maintain consistency in his rulings. As the sole judge hearing tariff refund cases, he has signalled that this approach will continue across all similar instances. The Trump administration's efforts to limit these refunds have been met with resistance from the court. The Justice Department has disputed the universal refund order, arguing that Judge Eaton exceeded his authority by issuing it without a court order. According to their filing, the Customs and Border Protection (CBP) lacks the power to reliquidate or refund money in such circumstances. The Trump administration's efforts to limit tariff refunds have encountered a significant hurdle in the courts. A recent Supreme Court decision has implications for the case at hand, as it limited the scope of universal injunctions in certain circumstances. Eaton's argument that the Supreme Court's limitations on universal injunctions do not apply to the Court of International Trade is based on the court's exclusive jurisdiction over trade issues and its unique operating procedures. This distinction may give Eaton a strong foundation for his case, as it sets the Court of International Trade apart from other courts in the country. The Democrats have made it clear that they intend to counter the Trump administration's efforts to impose new tariffs by using legislative means. Their first target is a repeal of specific levies on goods imported from Canada. Sen. Ron Wyden, who is set to take over as head of the Senate Finance Committee, is leading this effort and has been vocal in his opposition to the tariffs.
